title: Supporting Informed Choice and Person-Centered Planning
before: Explore how DSD staff explain meaningful options and chosen support so that a person’s own direction shapes planning.

turns.text: This course is Supporting Informed Choice and Person-Centered Planning. It’s about how we explain options and support so that a person’s own direction shapes their plan. It begins with a distinction I find useful in many conversations. Interest, a request for information, a preference, and agreement to an arrangement are different responses, even when they sound similar.

The course gives an example: “Are you okay with the program?” That question leaves a lot unclear, including what choice is being asked about and what the person would need to know. A person-centered starting point begins with the person’s life, strengths, priorities, and chosen relationships. A service menu is useful information, but it isn’t the whole goal.

The opening case shows how a form can shape that. A planning form lists a familiar service first and asks about community goals last. Staff start preparing that service before they’ve heard the person’s priorities. You’ll practice choosing a response. As you consider it, ask how hearing the goal first might change which options are worth examining.

Honesty about options is central here. Explain what each option involves, the relevant tradeoffs, and what remains unconfirmed. Don’t turn a possibility into an approved service, or an inquiry into a completed choice. Plain language helps only if it keeps the distinction the person needs in order to choose. A shorter explanation can still mislead.

Then there’s chosen help. Support may help a person compare information, ask questions, or communicate a choice, and the course asks us to clarify what help they want. Advice is different from authority, and a companion’s presence doesn’t automatically make them the decision-maker. Some people want a trusted person involved, while others prefer to compare privately.

That’s the third practice situation. A person asks a trusted supporter to help compare options, and the supporter picks one and communicates agreement before the person has decided. You’ll weigh how to restore the distinction. I also appreciate the reminder about tone. “That sounds fine” may be kindness while the person is still thinking, or it may be a choice.

So we shouldn’t assign agreement from tone or a presumed cultural pattern. The workplace example is a supervisor who assumes an employee with a disability wants a less demanding development path. Nobody has discussed the employee’s own goals. You’ll consider the best response. The course treats development goals as a matter of the employee’s preference, alongside the actual work expectations.

Risk is handled carefully, too. A preference may involve uncertainty or a tradeoff. The course asks us to explain relevant information and support without using concern to decide for the person. An unsupported promise isn’t choice, and an automatic protective refusal isn’t a complete assessment. Each can take the decision away from the person in a different way.

The course also looks at patterns. A default option, an incomplete explanation, or presumed incapacity can repeatedly limit whose preferences shape a plan. So it asks what was actually offered, what the person understood, and how their preference shaped the next step. Agreement, attendance, or a completed form alone can’t explain the quality of a choice.

People with disabilities and families can help examine whether planning explanations support actual choice, and their experiences may point to different gaps. Culture briefs prepare inquiry, but the person’s priorities stay specific to them. Near the end, you’ll privately revise a planning question so it identifies the choice, available help, and next effect without taking over the answer.

As you work through it, think of a question you often ask when someone is deciding something, whether in planning, supervision, or provider support. What choice does it actually put in front of the person? What would they need to know to answer it? Bring that question with you and see how it might change.

guidance.title: Starting with the person
guidance.text: When a service list comes first, the conversation tends to become about which item fits. Starting with what matters to the person changes the order of the questions. You learn about their priorities, their strengths, and the relationships they have chosen. Available support can then be explained in relation to those priorities, with an honest note about anything that is not yet confirmed.

guidance.title: The question you would ask
guidance.text: Look at the planning question you revised. Does it make clear what choice is being made and what happens next? Consider whether it leaves room for the person to want more information, more time, or a different kind of help. If someone answered “That sounds fine,” what follow-up question would help you understand what they meant?
